questiontext.text: In eukaryotic cells, the breakdown of complex molecules to yield energy takes place in which of the following cellular compartments?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of cellular sites for respiration
In eukaryotic organisms, photosynthetic food production occurs exclusively in chloroplasts. In contrast, the catabolic breakdown of complex carbon compounds to release energy occurs sequentially within the cytoplasm and the mitochondria.

Step 2: Pathway division
Glycolysis operates in the cytoplasm, whereas subsequent aerobic stages—the link reaction, citric acid cycle, and electron transport chain coupled to oxidative phosphorylation—occur inside mitochondria.

Step 3: Conclusion
The energy-yielding breakdown processes occur in the cytoplasm and mitochondria.

questiontext.text: Which of the following organic compounds is the most favoured and commonly oxidised respiratory substrate in living organisms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of respiratory substrates
During cellular respiration, organic compounds containing carbon-carbon bonds are oxidised to yield usable energy in the form of ATP. Although proteins, fats, and organic acids can enter the respiratory pathway under specific physiological conditions, carbohydrates—specifically glucose—are the primary and most favoured substrate.

Step 2: Conclusion
Carbohydrates represent the favoured and most common respiratory substrate.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Adaptation of plants lacking specialized respiratory organs

questiontext.text: Plants can get along without specialized respiratory organs like lungs or gills because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analysis of plant gaseous exchange
Plants do not possess dedicated respiratory organs due to several anatomical and physiological features: each plant part takes care of its own gas-exchange needs with minimal gas translocation, plant tissues respire at significantly lower rates than animals, and diffusion distances are very short because living cells lie close to the plant surface.

Step 2: Integration of features
Furthermore, loosely packed parenchyma cells provide an extensive, interconnected network of internal air spaces, facilitating direct diffusion across thin fluid-gas interfaces.

Step 3: Conclusion
Each plant organ takes care of its own gas-exchange needs, and diffusion distances for gases remain small.

answer.text: Each plant part takes care of its own gas-exchange needs, and diffusion distances are short
Plants have active bulk-flow circulatory systems for continuous oxygen delivery
All deep internal tissues of woody stems consist entirely of actively respiring living cells
Plant organs exhibit metabolic and respiratory rates much higher than those of mammals

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Organization of living cells in woody stems

questiontext.text: In bulky, thick woody stems, gas exchange with the atmosphere is facilitated because living cells are organized:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural anatomy of woody stems
In large woody stems and roots, the vast interior bulk consists of dead xylem elements that provide mechanical support without respiring.

Step 2: Location of metabolically active cells
The living cells are arranged in thin superficial layers beneath and inside the bark, in close proximity to lenticels and outer air spaces.

Step 3: Conclusion
Living cells form thin layers beneath and inside the bark, while the interior cells are largely dead.

answer.text: In thin layers beneath and inside the bark, with dead cells situated in the interior
Deep within the core heartwood surrounded by impermeable dead layers
Uniformly throughout the stem volume with no non-living elements present
Exclusively inside xylem tracheids and vessels to maximize liquid oxygen transport

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Conversion of sucrose prior to glycolysis

questiontext.text: In plants, sucrose derived from photosynthesis or storage tissues is converted into two hexose monosaccharides before entering glycolysis by the action of the enzyme:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Source of hexoses in plant respiration
In green plants, the primary transport disaccharide is sucrose. Before entering the glycolytic pathway, sucrose is hydrolysed into glucose and fructose.

Step 2: Enzyme identification
This hydrolytic reaction is catalysed by the enzyme invertase (sucrase), after which hexokinase phosphorylates both glucose and fructose into their respective phosphorylated forms.

Step 3: Conclusion
The enzyme responsible for splitting sucrose into glucose and fructose is invertase.

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the EMP pathway (glycolysis)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Key features of glycolysis
Glycolysis was elucidated by Embden, Meyerhof, and Parnas (EMP pathway). It takes place in the cytosol/cytoplasm of all living cells.

Step 2: Oxygen independence
Glycolysis does not require molecular oxygen; in obligate or facultative anaerobes, it is the sole respiratory pathway producing ATP.

Step 3: Conclusion
It occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms and functions independently of oxygen.

answer.text: It occurs in the cytoplasm of all living cells and does not consume molecular oxygen
It is confined exclusively to the mitochondrial matrix of eukaryotic organisms
It involves the complete oxidative breakdown of glucose into carbon dioxide and water
It occurs only in strictly aerobic cells and ceases completely under anaerobic conditions

questiontext.text: The phosphorylation of glucose to produce glucose-6-phosphate during the preparatory phase of glycolysis is catalysed by which enzyme?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Activation of glucose
Upon entering the cell, free glucose is phosphorylated using a molecule of ATP to form glucose-6-phosphate. This traps the sugar within the cytoplasm and initiates the glycolytic sequence.

Step 2: Enzyme identification
This priming phosphorylation reaction is catalysed by hexokinase.

Step 3: Conclusion
Hexokinase catalyses the initial phosphorylation of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate.

questiontext.text: During glycolysis, ATP is consumed at which two specific enzymatic conversion steps?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying ATP-consuming reactions in glycolysis
Glycolysis begins with an energy-investment phase where two ATP molecules are consumed per glucose molecule.

Step 2: Precise reactions
First: Conversion of Glucose into Glucose-6-phosphate (catalysed by hexokinase).
Second: Conversion of Fructose-6-phosphate into Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (catalysed by phosphofructokinase).

Step 3: Conclusion
ATP is consumed in the conversions: Glucose to Glucose-6-phosphate and Fructose-6-phosphate to Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.

answer.text: Glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, and fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
Glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, and triose phosphate to 2-phosphoglycerate
Fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, and PEP to pyruvic acid
1,3-bisphosphoglyceric acid to 3-phosphoglyceric acid, and PEP to pyruvic acid

questiontext.text: The six-carbon compound fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is cleaved during glycolysis into two interconvertible three-carbon triose phosphates named:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Splitting reaction in glycolysis
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (a 6-carbon phosphorylated sugar) is cleaved by aldolase into two isomeric 3-carbon phosphorylated sugars.

Step 2: Identification of triose phosphates
These two compounds are dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL, or glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate), which can isomerise into each other.

Step 3: Conclusion
The resulting triose phosphates are dihydroxyacetone phosphate and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde.

questiontext.text: At which step in the glycolytic pathway are reducing equivalents removed in the form of two hydrogen atoms to produce \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of the oxidation step in glycolysis
During the payoff phase, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (PGAL) undergoes oxidation coupled with phosphorylation.

Step 2: Electron and proton transfer
Two redox equivalents (two hydrogen atoms) are transferred from each PGAL molecule to \(\text{NAD}^+\), reducing it to \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\), while an inorganic phosphate (\(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\)) is incorporated to yield 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA).

Step 3: Conclusion
The formation of \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) occurs when 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL) is converted to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA).

questiontext.text: Substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis leading to direct synthesis of ATP occurs during which of the following reactions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying substrate-level phosphorylation reactions in glycolysis
Substrate-level phosphorylation refers to the direct synthesis of ATP from ADP by transfer of a phosphate group from a phosphorylated metabolic intermediate.

Step 2: Steps involved
In glycolysis, this happens at two steps:
1. 1,3-bisphosphoglyceric acid (BPGA) \(\rightarrow\) 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA)
2. Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) \(\rightarrow\) Pyruvic acid

Step 3: Conclusion
Both the conversion of BPGA to PGA and the conversion of PEP to pyruvic acid directly synthesise ATP.

answer.text: Conversion of BPGA to 3-PGA and conversion of PEP to pyruvic acid
Conversion of glucose to G-6-P and conversion of F-6-P to F-1,6-BP
Conversion of 3-PGA to 2-PGA and conversion of 2-PGA to PEP
Conversion of PGAL to BPGA and conversion of DHAP to PGAL

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q12 - Direct net ATP synthesis in glycolysis

questiontext.text: What is the net gain of ATP molecules directly synthesised via substrate-level phosphorylation from one molecule of glucose during glycolysis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Gross ATP production in glycolysis
One molecule of glucose yields two molecules of triose phosphate. Each triose phosphate generates two ATP molecules in the payoff phase: one during the conversion of BPGA to 3-PGA, and one during the conversion of PEP to pyruvate. Total gross ATP produced = \(2 \times 2 = 4\) ATP.

Step 2: ATP expenditure in glycolysis
Two ATP molecules are invested in the preparatory phase (glucose \(\rightarrow\) glucose-6-phosphate, and fructose-6-phosphate \(\rightarrow\) fructose-1,6-bisphosphate).

Step 3: Net calculation
\(\text{Net ATP} = 4 - 2 = 2\) ATP.

Step 4: Conclusion
The net gain of directly synthesised ATP molecules is 2.

questiontext.text: During glycolysis, the conversion of 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) involves the removal of which molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Enolase catalysed reaction
In the ninth step of glycolysis, 2-phosphoglycerate is converted to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) by the enzyme enolase.

Step 2: Nature of reaction
This reaction is a dehydration reaction involving the loss of a molecule of water (\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\)), creating a high-energy enol phosphate bond in PEP.

Step 3: Conclusion
Water (\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\)) is eliminated during the conversion of 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q14 - Number of carbon atoms in glycolytic intermediates

questiontext.text:
Consider the following glycolytic intermediates:
(i) Dihydroxyacetone phosphate
(ii) Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
(iii) Phosphoenolpyruvate
(iv) Pyruvic acid
Which of the following correctly matches the number of carbon atoms present in each molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Carbon count for each compound
- Dihydroxyacetone phosphate: 3-carbon triose phosphate (3C)
- Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate: 6-carbon hexose bisphosphate (6C)
- Phosphoenolpyruvate: 3-carbon organic acid precursor (3C)
- Pyruvic acid: 3-carbon alpha-keto acid (3C)

Step 2: Conclusion
The correct carbon numbers are (i) 3, (ii) 6, (iii) 3, (iv) 3.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q15 - Fate of pyruvic acid under anaerobic conditions

questiontext.text: In yeast cells, the anaerobic conversion of pyruvic acid to ethanol and carbon dioxide is catalysed sequentially by which two enzymes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Alcoholic fermentation mechanism
Under anaerobic conditions in yeast, pyruvate undergoes fermentation.

Step 2: Identification of enzymes
First, pyruvic acid is decarboxylated into acetaldehyde and carbon dioxide by the enzyme pyruvic acid decarboxylase. Second, acetaldehyde is reduced to ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase with the simultaneous oxidation of \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) to \(\text{NAD}^+\).

Step 3: Conclusion
The two enzymes involved are pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q16 - Reducing agent in lactic acid fermentation

questiontext.text: During lactic acid fermentation in animal muscle cells under oxygen deficit, the reducing agent that reduces pyruvic acid to lactic acid is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of lactic acid formation
During strenuous muscular exercise, when oxygen supply is insufficient, pyruvate is reduced to lactic acid by the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase.

Step 2: Source of reducing equivalents
The electron donor (reducing agent) is \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\), which is re-oxidised to \(\text{NAD}^+\), regenerating the pool of \(\text{NAD}^+\) required to maintain glycolytic ATP generation.

Step 3: Conclusion
The reducing agent is \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\).

questiontext.text: In both lactic acid and alcoholic fermentation, the proportion of total energy present in glucose that is released is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Energy efficiency of fermentation
Fermentation represents an incomplete oxidation of glucose under anaerobic conditions.

Step 2: Quantitative percentage
According to NCERT, less than 7 per cent of the total energy contained in the glucose molecule is released during fermentation, and not all of that released energy is trapped in high-energy bonds of ATP.

Step 3: Conclusion
The energy released is less than 7 per cent.

questiontext.text: Yeast cells poison themselves to death when the concentration of alcohol reaches approximately what percentage during natural fermentation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of alcoholic toxicity
During natural fermentation by yeast, ethanol accumulates in the medium. When the concentration reaches about 13 per cent, it becomes toxic and causes yeast cell death.

Step 2: Application to beverages
Beverages with higher alcohol concentrations (such as whiskey, rum, or brandy) must be produced through distillation rather than natural fermentation alone.

Step 3: Conclusion
The threshold is about 13 per cent.

questiontext.text: Which of the following comparisons between fermentation and aerobic respiration is correct regarding the oxidation of \(\text{NADH}\) to \(\text{NAD}^+\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Rate of NADH reoxidation
In fermentation, the re-oxidation of \(\text{NADH}\) to \(\text{NAD}^+\) occurs rather slowly as it transfers electrons directly to organic intermediates (such as pyruvate or acetaldehyde) in the cytoplasm.

Step 2: Aerobic condition
In aerobic respiration, \(\text{NADH}\) donates electrons into the mitochondrial electron transport system, where the oxidation reaction is very vigorous.

Step 3: Conclusion
\(\text{NADH}\) is oxidised to \(\text{NAD}^+\) slowly in fermentation, but the reaction is vigorous in aerobic respiration.

answer.text: \(\text{NADH}\) is oxidised to \(\text{NAD}^+\) slowly in fermentation, but vigorously in aerobic respiration
\(\text{NADH}\) is oxidised to \(\text{NAD}^+\) vigorously in fermentation, but extremely slowly in aerobic respiration
Oxidation of \(\text{NADH}\) occurs at identical rates in both fermentation and aerobic respiration
\(\text{NADH}\) is never re-oxidised to \(\text{NAD}^+\) in fermentation processes

questiontext.text: A crucial biochemical difference between lactic acid fermentation and alcoholic fermentation is that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Chemical reactions of both fermentations
- Alcoholic fermentation: \(\text{Pyruvic acid} \xrightarrow{\text{decarboxylase}} \text{Acetaldehyde} + \text{CO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{dehydrogenase}} \text{Ethanol}\). Carbon dioxide is released.
- Lactic acid fermentation: \(\text{Pyruvic acid} + \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+ \xrightarrow{\text{lactate dehydrogenase}} \text{Lactic acid} + \text{NAD}^+\). No decarboxylation occurs.

Step 2: Conclusion
Carbon dioxide is released in alcoholic fermentation, but not in lactic acid fermentation.

answer.text: \(\text{CO}_2\) is released during alcoholic fermentation, but not during lactic acid fermentation
\(\text{CO}_2\) is released during lactic acid fermentation, but not during alcoholic fermentation
\(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) is consumed only in lactic acid fermentation and not in alcoholic fermentation
Lactic acid fermentation yields four net ATP molecules while alcoholic fermentation yields none

questiontext.text: In eukaryotic aerobic respiration, where do (i) complete oxidation of pyruvate by stepwise removal of hydrogen atoms and (ii) electron transfer to molecular \(\text{O}_2\) coupled with ATP synthesis take place?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Separation of crucial events
Aerobic respiration involves two major spatial compartments inside mitochondria:
- First event: Oxidation of pyruvate by stepwise removal of hydrogen atoms, releasing three \(\text{CO}_2\) molecules, takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.
- Second event: Passing of electrons removed with hydrogen atoms to \(\text{O}_2\) with simultaneous ATP synthesis takes place on the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Step 2: Conclusion
The matrix of mitochondria hosts the first event, while the inner mitochondrial membrane hosts the second event.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q22 - Cofactor in oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate

questiontext.text: The oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvic acid to form acetyl CoA is catalysed by pyruvate dehydrogenase and specifically requires which divalent cation as a cofactor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analysis of the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction
The oxidative decarboxylation reaction is written as:
\(\text{Pyruvic acid} + \text{CoA} + \text{NAD}^+ \xrightarrow[\text{Pyruvate dehydrogenase}]{\text{Mg}^{2+}} \text{Acetyl CoA} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\)

Step 2: Identification of cofactor
The enzyme complex requires the divalent magnesium cation (\(\text{Mg}^{2+}\)) alongside coenzymes including \(\text{NAD}^+\) and Coenzyme A.

Step 3: Conclusion
The required divalent cation is \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q23 - Yield of NADH from link reaction

questiontext.text: How many molecules of \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and \(\text{CO}_2\) are produced during the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvic acid per glucose molecule metabolised?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Stoichiometry per glucose molecule
One molecule of glucose yields two molecules of pyruvic acid via glycolysis.

Step 2: Yield from oxidative decarboxylation
Each pyruvic acid molecule produces 1 \(\text{CO}_2\) and 1 \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) upon conversion to acetyl CoA.
Therefore, two molecules of pyruvic acid produce 2 molecules of \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and 2 molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\).

Step 3: Conclusion
2 \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and 2 \(\text{CO}_2\) are formed.

questiontext.text: The tricarboxylic acid cycle begins with the condensation of an acetyl group with oxaloacetic acid and water to yield citric acid. This initial reaction is catalysed by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the entry reaction of TCA cycle
Acetyl CoA (a 2-carbon unit) condenses with oxaloacetic acid (a 4-carbon dicarboxylic acid) in the presence of water.

Step 2: Enzyme catalysis
This condensation reaction is catalysed by citrate synthase, producing citric acid (a 6-carbon tricarboxylic acid) and releasing free Coenzyme A (CoA).

Step 3: Conclusion
Citrate synthase catalyses this reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q25 - Number of carbon atoms in alpha ketoglutaric acid

questiontext.text: How many carbon atoms are present in an \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid molecule formed during the TCA cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Carbon sequence in Krebs cycle
Citrate (6C) is isomerised to isocitrate (6C). Isocitrate then undergoes its first oxidative decarboxylation with the loss of one molecule of \(\text{CO}_2\).

Step 2: Carbon counting
\(6\text{ carbons} - 1\text{ carbon} (\text{as }\text{CO}_2) = 5\text{ carbons}\). The resulting intermediate is \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid.

Step 3: Conclusion
\(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid contains 5 carbon atoms.

questiontext.text: During one complete turn of the TCA cycle (from acetyl CoA), how many molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) are released?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Tracing decarboxylation steps in TCA cycle
During one turn of the TCA cycle, two successive oxidative decarboxylations occur:
1. Isocitrate (6C) \(\rightarrow\) \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid (5C) + \(\text{CO}_2\)
2. \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid (5C) \(\rightarrow\) Succinyl-CoA (4C) + \(\text{CO}_2\)

Step 2: Conclusion
A total of 2 molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) are released during one turn of the TCA cycle.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q27 - Substrate level phosphorylation in TCA cycle

questiontext.text: Substrate-level phosphorylation in the Krebs' cycle takes place during the conversion of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying substrate-level phosphorylation in Krebs cycle
In the citric acid cycle, a nucleoside triphosphate is synthesised directly by the cleavage of a high-energy thioester bond.

Step 2: Conversion reaction
This occurs during the conversion of succinyl-CoA into succinic acid, where a molecule of GTP is synthesised from GDP and inorganic phosphate, which is coupled to ATP synthesis.

Step 3: Conclusion
The reaction is the conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinic acid.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q28 - Step of FADH2 generation in TCA cycle

questiontext.text: In the citric acid cycle, reduction of \(\text{FAD}^+\) to \(\text{FADH}_2\) occurs during the oxidation of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the FAD reduction reaction
In the TCA cycle, there is only one specific step where flavin adenine dinucleotide (\(\text{FAD}^+\)) is reduced to \(\text{FADH}_2\).

Step 2: Substrate conversion
This occurs during the oxidation of succinic acid (succinate) to fumaric acid (fumarate), catalysed by succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II of ETS).

Step 3: Conclusion
\(\text{FADH}_2\) is generated during the conversion of succinic acid to fumaric acid (or malic acid precursor).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q29 - Coenzyme reduction points in TCA cycle

questiontext.text: During a single turn of the citric acid cycle (starting from acetyl-CoA), what are the total numbers of \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\) generated?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying reduction steps in one turn of the TCA cycle
In one turn of the citric acid cycle:
- \(\text{NAD}^+\) is reduced to \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) at three steps:
1. Isocitrate \(\rightarrow\) \(\alpha\)-ketoglutarate
2. \(\alpha\)-ketoglutarate \(\rightarrow\) Succinyl-CoA
3. Malate \(\rightarrow\) Oxaloacetate
- \(\text{FAD}^+\) is reduced to \(\text{FADH}_2\) at one step: Succinate \(\rightarrow\) Fumarate

Step 2: Conclusion
There are 3 molecules of \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and 1 molecule of \(\text{FADH}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q30 - Total NADH and FADH2 from one glucose in TCA and link

questiontext.text: Starting from one molecule of glucose, how many total molecules of \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\) are formed exclusively inside the mitochondrial matrix prior to the electron transport chain?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Yield from oxidative decarboxylation (link reaction)
One glucose yields two pyruvates. In the mitochondrial matrix, these two pyruvates undergo oxidative decarboxylation to produce 2 \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\).

Step 2: Yield from TCA cycle
The two resulting molecules of acetyl CoA enter two cycles of the TCA pathway in the matrix, producing \(2 \times 3 = 6\) \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and \(2 \times 1 = 2\) \(\text{FADH}_2\).

Step 3: Total mitochondrial matrix yield
Total \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+ = 2 + 6 = 8\).
Total \(\text{FADH}_2 = 2\).

Step 4: Conclusion
The totals are 8 \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and 2 \(\text{FADH}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q31 - Identity of Complex I in ETS

questiontext.text: In the inner mitochondrial membrane, Complex I of the electron transport system is known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of ETS complexes
The respiratory electron transport system comprises five multi-protein complexes embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Step 2: Complex I identity
Complex I oxidises matrix-derived \(\text{NADH}\) and transfers electrons via FMN and Fe-S centres to ubiquinone; it is named NADH dehydrogenase.

Step 3: Conclusion
Complex I is NADH dehydrogenase.

questiontext.text: In the mitochondrial electron transport system, ubiquinone receives reducing equivalents directly from which complexes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role of ubiquinone (UQ)
Ubiquinone is a lipid-soluble mobile electron carrier located within the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Step 2: Dual convergence on UQ
- It receives electrons from matrix \(\text{NADH}\) through Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase).
- It also receives reducing equivalents via \(\text{FADH}_2\) generated during the oxidation of succinate through Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase).
Both donate electrons to convert ubiquinone to ubiquinol (\(\text{UQH}_2\)).

Step 3: Conclusion
Ubiquinone receives reducing equivalents from both Complex I and Complex II.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q33 - Mobile carrier between Complex III and IV

questiontext.text: Which of the following acts as a small, mobile electron carrier protein attached to the outer surface of the inner mitochondrial membrane to transfer electrons between Complex III and Complex IV?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the mobile carrier
Electrons from ubiquinol pass to Complex III (cytochrome \(bc_1\) complex), which in turn transfers them to cytochrome \(c\).

Step 2: Characteristics of cytochrome c
Cytochrome \(c\) is a small peripheral protein attached to the outer surface of the inner mitochondrial membrane that shuttles electrons between Complex III and Complex IV (cytochrome \(c\) oxidase).

Step 3: Conclusion
Cytochrome \(c\) acts as the mobile carrier between Complex III and IV.

questiontext.text: Complex IV of the mitochondrial electron transport chain refers to cytochrome \(c\) oxidase, which contains:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural composition of Complex IV
Complex IV is cytochrome \(c\) oxidase.

Step 2: Prosthetic groups and centres
It comprises two heme-containing cytochromes, cytochrome \(a\) and cytochrome \(a_3\), along with two copper centres (\(\text{Cu}_A\) and \(\text{Cu}_B\)).

Step 3: Conclusion
Complex IV contains cytochromes \(a\) and \(a_3\), and two copper centres.

questiontext.text: During aerobic respiration, the terminal electron and hydrogen acceptor in the electron transport chain is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role of oxygen in aerobic respiration
Although oxygen enters only at the terminal stage of ETS, its presence is indispensable because it drives the entire electron transport process by continuously clearing electrons and protons from the terminal carrier.

Step 2: Reduction of oxygen
Molecular oxygen acts as the final electron/hydrogen acceptor, combining with protons to form water: \(\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}\).

Step 3: Conclusion
Molecular oxygen (\(\text{O}_2\)) is the terminal electron acceptor.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q36 - Theoretical ATP yield from NADH and FADH2

questiontext.text: According to the standard respiratory balance sheet described in NCERT, the complete oxidation of one molecule of \(\text{NADH}\) and one molecule of \(\text{FADH}_2\) through the ETS yields, respectively:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Proton pumping and ATP yield from electron donors
Electrons from \(\text{NADH}\) enter at Complex I and traverse three proton-pumping complexes (Complexes I, III, and IV), generating a larger proton gradient equivalent to 3 ATP molecules.

Step 2: FADH2 entry point
Electrons from \(\text{FADH}_2\) enter downstream at Complex II, bypassing Complex I, and therefore traverse only two proton-pumping complexes (Complexes III and IV), giving rise to 2 ATP molecules.

Step 3: Conclusion
One molecule of \(\text{NADH}\) yields 3 ATP, while one molecule of \(\text{FADH}_2\) yields 2 ATP.

questiontext.text: In ATP synthase (Complex V) of the inner mitochondrial membrane, the catalytic site for ATP synthesis from ADP and inorganic phosphate is located on the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural components of Complex V
ATP synthase consists of two distinct functional parts:
- \(F_0\): an integral membrane protein complex forming a transmembrane channel through which protons cross the inner mitochondrial membrane down their electrochemical gradient.
- \(F_1\): a peripheral membrane protein headpiece that protrudes into the mitochondrial matrix.

Step 2: Catalytic site location
The catalytic site for phosphorylation of ADP with inorganic phosphate to synthesize ATP resides on the \(F_1\) headpiece.

Step 3: Conclusion
The catalytic site is located on the \(F_1\) peripheral headpiece.

answer.text: \(F_0\) integral channel embedded in the membrane

questiontext.text: According to the NCERT textbook, for each molecule of ATP produced by ATP synthase in the mitochondria, how many protons (\(\text{H}^+\)) pass through \(F_0\) from the intermembrane space to the matrix down the electrochemical gradient?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: NCERT Chemiosmotic coupling ratio
The chemiosmotic hypothesis describes the translocation of protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane via Complex V.

Step 2: Specific proton requirement
NCERT explicitly states: "For each ATP produced, \(4\text{H}^+\) pass through \(F_0\) from the intermembrane space to the matrix down the electrochemical proton gradient."

Step 3: Conclusion
The number of protons translocated per ATP produced is 4.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q39 - Net theoretical ATP gain from one glucose

questiontext.text: Under the theoretical assumptions of the complete respiratory balance sheet (sequential pathway, complete transfer of glycolytic NADH, and unbranched metabolism), the net gain of ATP molecules during aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Balance sheet summation
- Glycolysis: 2 direct ATP + 2 \(\text{NADH}\) (\(2 \times 3 = 6\) ATP) = 8 ATP
- Link reaction: 2 \(\text{NADH}\) (\(2 \times 3 = 6\) ATP) = 6 ATP
- Krebs cycle: 2 direct GTP (ATP) + 6 \(\text{NADH}\) (\(6 \times 3 = 18\) ATP) + 2 \(\text{FADH}_2\) (\(2 \times 2 = 4\) ATP) = 24 ATP

Step 2: Total calculation
Total net ATP = \(8 + 6 + 24 = 38\) ATP.

Step 3: Conclusion
The net gain under these theoretical assumptions is 38 ATP molecules.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q40 - Point of entry of glycerol into respiration

questiontext.text: When fats are utilised as respiratory substrates, they are first hydrolysed into fatty acids and glycerol. Glycerol enters the respiratory pathway after being converted into:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Breakdown of lipids for respiration
Fats are broken down by lipases into glycerol and fatty acids.

Step 2: Fate of glycerol
Glycerol is a 3-carbon polyol. It enters the glycolytic pathway after phosphorylation and oxidation to 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL).

Step 3: Conclusion
Glycerol enters after conversion into PGAL (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q41 - Entry point of fatty acids into respiration

questiontext.text: If fatty acids are to be respired as an energy source, they are broken down and enter the respiratory pathway as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fatty acid oxidation
Fatty acids undergo beta-oxidation to generate 2-carbon units.

Step 2: Entry point
These 2-carbon units are in the form of acetyl CoA, which enters directly into the Krebs' cycle in the mitochondrial matrix.

Step 3: Conclusion
Fatty acids enter the pathway as acetyl CoA.

questiontext.text: Why is the respiratory pathway more appropriately termed an amphibolic pathway rather than purely a catabolic pathway?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Meaning of catabolism and anabolism
Catabolism refers to degradation or breakdown reactions releasing energy, while anabolism refers to synthetic processes requiring energy and building blocks.

Step 2: Dual role of the respiratory pathway
The respiratory pathway breaks down carbohydrates, fats, and proteins (catabolism). However, intermediates of the pathway are withdrawn for biosynthesis (anabolism)—for instance, acetyl CoA is withdrawn to synthesize fatty acids, and Krebs cycle keto-acids are withdrawn to synthesize amino acids.

Step 3: Conclusion
Because the pathway is involved in both catabolism (breakdown) and anabolism (synthesis), it is termed amphibolic.

answer.text: Its intermediates are utilised in both catabolic breakdown and anabolic biosynthetic reactions
It can proceed in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions without enzymes
It generates equal amounts of heat energy and chemical energy at every step
It occurs simultaneously in chloroplasts and peroxisomes in all plant cells

questiontext.text: When glucose is completely oxidised aerobically as the sole respiratory substrate, the Respiratory Quotient (RQ) is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of RQ
\(\text{RQ} = \frac{\text{Volume of }\text{CO}_2\text{ evolved}}{\text{Volume of }\text{O}_2\text{ consumed}}\)

Step 2: Aerobic oxidation of glucose
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2 \longrightarrow 6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Energy}\)

Step 3: Calculating ratio
\(\text{RQ} = \frac{6\text{CO}_2}{6\text{O}_2} = 1.0\)

Step 4: Conclusion
The RQ for carbohydrate oxidation is 1.0.

questiontext.text:
The balanced chemical equation for the respiratory breakdown of the fatty acid tripalmitin is:
\[2(\text{C}_{51}\text{H}_{98}\text{O}_6) + 145\text{O}_2 \longrightarrow 102\text{CO}_2 + 98\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Energy}\]
What is the Respiratory Quotient (RQ) for tripalmitin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formula for RQ
\(\text{RQ} = \frac{\text{Volume of }\text{CO}_2\text{ evolved}}{\text{Volume of }\text{O}_2\text{ consumed}}\)

Step 2: Numerical evaluation
From the balanced reaction:
Moles of \(\text{CO}_2\) evolved = 102
Moles of \(\text{O}_2\) consumed = 145
\(\text{RQ} = \frac{102}{145} \approx 0.7\)

Step 3: Conclusion
The Respiratory Quotient of tripalmitin is 0.7.

questiontext.text: When proteins are used as respiratory substrates, the value of the Respiratory Quotient (RQ) is approximately:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understanding protein oxidation
Proteins are polymers of amino acids. Because proteins contain relatively more oxygen-poor hydrocarbon residues compared to carbohydrates, more oxygen is consumed relative to carbon dioxide produced.

Step 2: NCERT value
NCERT explicitly specifies that when proteins are respiratory substrates, the respiratory ratio is about 0.9.

Step 3: Conclusion
The approximate RQ for proteins is 0.9.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q46 - Total CO2 molecules from one glucose

questiontext.text: During complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule, how many total molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) are produced, and at which stages are they released?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying stages of carbon dioxide release
- Glycolysis: Glucose (6C) is cleaved into 2 Pyruvate (3C). No \(\text{CO}_2\) is released (0 \(\text{CO}_2\)).
- Link Reaction: 2 Pyruvate (3C) \(\rightarrow\) 2 Acetyl CoA (2C) + 2 \(\text{CO}_2\). (2 \(\text{CO}_2\) released).
- Krebs Cycle: 2 Acetyl CoA (2C) \(\rightarrow\) 4 \(\text{CO}_2\) through two turns of TCA cycle. (4 \(\text{CO}_2\) released).

Step 2: Total summation
Total \(\text{CO}_2\) released = \(0 + 2 + 4 = 6\) molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\).

Step 3: Conclusion
6 molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) are released: 2 during the link reaction and 4 during the Krebs' cycle.

answer.text: 6 \(\text{CO}_2\); 2 during oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate and 4 during the Krebs' cycle
6 \(\text{CO}_2\); 2 during glycolysis, 2 during the link reaction, and 2 during the Krebs' cycle
4 \(\text{CO}_2\); all 4 released exclusively in the citric acid cycle
3 \(\text{CO}_2\); 1 during the link reaction and 2 during the Krebs' cycle

questiontext.text: What fundamental energy difference distinguishes oxidative phosphorylation in respiration from photophosphorylation in photosynthesis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Energy driver in photophosphorylation
In photophosphorylation, light energy is captured by pigments to excite electrons and create a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane.

Step 2: Energy driver in oxidative phosphorylation
In oxidative phosphorylation, the energy released from oxidation-reduction reactions (electron transfer from NADH/FADH2 to oxygen) is utilised to pump protons and establish the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Step 3: Conclusion
Oxidative phosphorylation utilises oxidation-reduction energy, whereas photophosphorylation utilises light energy.

answer.text: Oxidative phosphorylation utilizes oxidation-reduction energy, whereas photophosphorylation utilizes light energy
Oxidative phosphorylation does not require a membrane-associated proton gradient
Photophosphorylation occurs across the inner mitochondrial membrane
Oxidative phosphorylation synthesises GTP rather than ATP

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATION_IN_PLANTS_MCQ_Q48 - Sequence of electron transport through ETS complexes

questiontext.text: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of electron transfer from \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) along the complexes of the electron transport system to oxygen?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identifying the entry and pathway for NADH electrons
Electrons from mitochondrial matrix \(\text{NADH}\) enter at Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase).

Step 2: Subsequent sequence
1. From Complex I, electrons pass to Ubiquinone (UQ).
2. Ubiquinol (\(\text{UQH}_2\)) transfers electrons to Complex III (cytochrome \(bc_1\) complex).
3. Complex III passes electrons to the mobile carrier cytochrome \(c\).
4. Cytochrome \(c\) delivers electrons to Complex IV (cytochrome \(c\) oxidase).
5. Complex IV transfers electrons to molecular oxygen, forming \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\).

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct sequence is: Complex I \(\rightarrow\) Ubiquinone \(\rightarrow\) Complex III \(\rightarrow\) Cytochrome \(c\) \(\rightarrow\) Complex IV \(\rightarrow\) \(\text{O}_2\).

answer.text: Complex I \(\rightarrow\) Ubiquinone \(\rightarrow\) Complex III \(\rightarrow\) Cytochrome \(c\) \(\rightarrow\) Complex IV \(\rightarrow\) \(\text{O}_2\)
Complex I \(\rightarrow\) Complex II \(\rightarrow\) Cytochrome \(c\) \(\rightarrow\) Complex III \(\rightarrow\) Complex IV \(\rightarrow\) \(\text{O}_2\)
Complex II \(\rightarrow\) Ubiquinone \(\rightarrow\) Complex I \(\rightarrow\) Complex III \(\rightarrow\) Complex IV \(\rightarrow\) \(\text{O}_2\)
Complex I \(\rightarrow\) Cytochrome \(c\) \(\rightarrow\) Complex III \(\rightarrow\) Ubiquinone \(\rightarrow\) Complex IV \(\rightarrow\) \(\text{O}_2\)
